summary:
This evaluation covered 8 evals over 3 iterations each (33 total runs, no run failures). Five of the eight evals ("unrelated-*") were negative-control tasks where the trigger was correctly NOT expected to fire content — both variants correctly avoided triggering full behavior (trigger_fired 3/3 for all), and expected_output/assertions/comparison/consistency were all marked skipped by design. These are not data points favoring either variant; they simply confirm both variants behave correctly on out-of-scope inputs.

The three substantive evals ("firehose-review-trigger", "firehose-review-severity-definitions", "firehose-review-pillars") all had the trigger fire 3/3 for both variants, but show a stark and consistent split in expected-output and assertion pass rates, with with_skill passing far more often:

- **firehose-review-severity-definitions**: with_skill passed expected_output 3/3 (100%) and all 18/18 assertions (100%, high confidence); without_skill passed 0/3 expected_output and 0/12 assertions. Every individual assertion (severity levels listed, correct ordering) shows the same pattern: with_skill passes, without_skill fails. with_skill's output was also rated fully "consistent" across runs. without_skill ran with ~0s runtime/$0 cost, suggesting it may not have produced substantive output at all in this eval, which likely explains the complete assertion failure.
- **firehose-review-pillars**: same pattern — with_skill 3/3 expected_output and 21/21 assertions (100%, high confidence); without_skill 0/3 expected_output and 0/21 assertions, again failing every individual pillar-naming assertion. Runtime and cost were comparable between variants here (~4s, ~$0.03-0.04). Output consistency was "mostly_consistent" for both (with_skill score 2.0 with one dimension flagged inconsistent; without_skill score 2.67, slightly more consistent).
- **firehose-review-trigger**: more mixed. with_skill passed expected_output 2/3 (67%, medium confidence) vs without_skill 1/3 (33%, high confidence). Aggregate assertions: with_skill 7/12 (58%) vs without_skill 3/6 (50%) — closer here than the other two evals. Looking at individual assertions: two always pass for both (framing as a review, severity rating present — these don't differentiate the variants), one always fails for both (DataFreshness/delivery-lag signal — a gap in both variants or the assertion itself), one is flaky for both (pillar organization). But two assertions split by variant: "scope establishment" passes only for without_skill and fails for with_skill, while "severity level named (regex)" passes only for with_skill and fails for without_skill — so each variant has a distinct strength here. On this eval, quality comparison (only 1 of 3 pairs evaluated, 2 skipped, medium confidence) favored without_skill on accuracy, actionability, and completeness. without_skill was also notably faster (2m47s vs 5m19s) and cheaper ($1.39 vs $2.65) on this eval.

Overall pattern: on two of the three substantive evals, with_skill's expected-output and assertion pass rates are dramatically and unambiguously higher (100% vs 0%), often at high confidence, indicating without_skill failed to produce the expected content in those cases (consistent with near-zero runtime/cost recorded for without_skill on one of them). On the third eval, results are more balanced, with each variant winning different individual assertions and the limited quality comparison (only 1 pair, medium confidence) favoring without_skill, while without_skill was faster and cheaper. Quality comparisons overall rest on very few evaluated pairs (0-1 per eval, with 2-3 skipped each time), so confidence in the quality dimension specifically is low. No evals showed both variants failing broadly except for isolated always-failing assertions (e.g., DataFreshness signal), which likely point to a gap in both variants or the assertion criterion itself.

firehose-review-trigger.summary:
This eval covers a single chat task where the agent was expected to perform a Firehose operational/best-practices review. The trigger condition fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the behavior under test was reliably exercised.

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in 2 of 3 runs (67%, medium confidence), without_skill in 1 of 3 (33%, high confidence). This favors with_skill numerically, though the sample size is only 3 runs per variant, so this should be read as a modest, low-n signal rather than a firm result.

Assertion-level detail (note with_skill had 12 assertion instances vs without_skill's 6, reflecting the 3 vs fewer runs where assertions applied): overall pass rates were close — with_skill 58% (7/12), without_skill 50% (3/6). Looking at individual assertions:
- Two assertions passed consistently for both variants ("frames work as Firehose review", "explicit severity rating") — these aren't distinguishing the variants.
- One assertion ("references DataFreshness/delivery-lag as a signal") failed for both variants entirely — this suggests either the assertion or the underlying behavior needs attention regardless of variant.
- One assertion ("organized by Well-Architected pillar") was flaky for both, passing only partially (with_skill 1/2, without_skill 0/1).
- One assertion ("asks for/establishes scope before reviewing") passed for without_skill (1/1) but failed for with_skill (0/2) — a clear divergence favoring without_skill.
- Another assertion ("names at least one severity level", regex-based) passed for with_skill (2/2) but failed for without_skill (0/1) — a divergence favoring with_skill.
So the two variants each have one assertion where they uniquely succeed and the other fails, roughly offsetting each other.

Quality comparison: only 1 pair was evaluated (2 pairs were skipped, limiting confidence), and in that single pair without_skill was favored across all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), at medium confidence. Given only one comparable pair, this is a thin data point and shouldn't be over-weighted.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took ~5m19s and cost ~$2.65 on average; without_skill took ~2m47s and cost ~$1.39 — roughly half the time and cost. Context window utilization was low for both (7.3% vs 4.3%), with no compaction events for either. One runtime pair exceeded the 30-second threshold in the runtime comparison, though with only 1 pair evaluated this is limited evidence.

Output consistency across repeated runs was not available (null) for either variant, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, the picture is mixed rather than one-sided: with_skill shows a higher expected-output match rate and a slight edge in aggregate assertion pass rate, plus a unique assertion win, but takes roughly twice as long and costs about twice as much as without_skill. without_skill shows a unique assertion win of its own and was favored in the single quality-comparison pair, but with only one pair evaluated that finding is low-confidence. Several assertions (shared passes, shared failures) don't differentiate the variants at all, and the small number of runs/pairs throughout means these differences should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs converge on the same core facts (zero traffic on all 4 streams, broken IAM role on iceberg-logs-stream200, SSE disabled fleet-wide, missing tags, quota headroom). However, Output B provides more granular and verifiable specifics: exact stream names, destinations, creation dates, exact role names for the over-permissioned IAM grant (FirehoseIcebergDeliveryRole vs Role400), specific quota numbers (500,000 rec/sec, 5 MiB/sec, 2,000 PUT/sec), and a specific note about the Iceberg AppendOnly throughput cap in us-east-1 which is a real, documented Firehose limitation. It also correctly identifies a 5th stream that appears in historical metrics as already deleted, showing more thorough data reconciliation. Output A's claim that 'No distinct Iceberg-specific quota code was returned' is vaguer and potentially less accurate than B's specific quota details. Output A also lists an extra pillar (Sustainability) with essentially no substantive finding, which adds structure but no verified content. Output A's IAM over-permission claim on lakeformation:GetDataAccess for stream400's role isn't cross-checked against B's more specific glue:GetTable*/UpdateTable finding, but B's specificity (contrasting Role vs Role400) suggests deeper investigation.
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'Note: the Iceberg destination cap in us-east-1 is 5 MiB/sec unless AppendOnly is enabled...' and 'Provisioned per-stream throughput is elevated above documented defaults (500,000 rec/sec, 5 MiB/sec, and 2,000 PUT/sec...)'. Output A: 'No distinct Iceberg-specific quota code was returned by Service Quotas for this account/region — only the general per-stream limits apply.'

criteria.reasoning: Both provide severity-rated findings with clear next steps. Output A ends with a clear 'Priority order' list (1-4) which is a strong actionability feature, and offers to generate a report artifact or investigate CloudTrail for the role deletion — good proactive follow-up options. Output B embeds 'Action:' directly within the critical finding and provides specific, concrete remediation guidance for each finding (e.g., 'confirm with owning team whether upstream producer is silently failing... or whether these are dead streams that should be deleted', specific role/prefix issues to fix). B also flags additional actionable items A misses entirely (empty S3 backup prefixes causing triage issues at bucket root, unused AWS-template policy needing trimming, deleted stream needing no action). While A has a cleaneer prioritized list, B's findings themselves contain more specific, directly actionable remediation detail per bullet, and covers more distinct actionable issues.
criteria.evidence: Output B: '**Action:** confirm with the owning team whether an upstream producer is silently failing to send data, or whether these are dead streams that should be deleted.' Output A: '1. **CRITICAL** — Recreate `FirehoseIcebergDeliveryRole100` (or repoint the stream)... 2. **HIGH** — Enable SSE on all 4 streams...'

criteria.reasoning: Output A organizes findings by pillar (Security, Reliability, Performance, Quotas, Cost, Operational Excellence, Sustainability) which maps well to the requested review structure, and explicitly names 6 of the requested pillars plus an extra one. However, several pillar cells contain sparse or filler content (e.g., Sustainability pillar has almost no independent finding, just cross-references). Output B does not explicitly label 'pillars' matching the request (security, reliability, delivery health, performance, cost, quotas) but instead organizes by severity, and within that structure it actually covers more distinct topics: broken IAM role, retry duration, encryption, disabled logging, empty S3 prefixes, compression/partitioning, IAM over-permission specifics, backup mode, tagging/clutter, unused policy, and detailed quota/throughput analysis including the Iceberg AppendOnly cap — effectively covering security, reliability, delivery health, performance, cost, and quotas within its severity-based structure, and arguably with more depth per topic than Output A. Output A explicitly maps to the requested categories more directly (better structural completeness against the literal ask), but Output B has more substantive coverage of each topic's nuances. This is a closer call, but B edges out due to greater depth of distinct findings under each implied category.
criteria.evidence: Output A pillar table explicitly labeled by pillar name matching the prompt's ask (Security, Reliability, Performance, Service Quotas, Cost, Operational Excellence, Sustainability). Output B severity-based structure covers: IAM role broken + retry duration (reliability), encryption (security), CloudWatch logging (delivery health/observability), empty S3 prefixes (delivery health), compression/partitioning (cost), IAM over-permission (security), backup mode (reliability/security), tagging (governance), quotas with specific throughput numbers and Iceberg cap details (quotas).

firehose-review-severity-definitions.summary:
This eval tested a chat task about listing five severity levels in order (most to least urgent), with expectations that CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, and INFO all appear and be correctly ordered.

The behavior under test fired for all 3 runs (trigger_fired 3/3) for both variants, so the eval was actually exercised.

On expected-output match and per-assertion pass rates, the two variants diverged sharply: with_skill met the expected output in all 3/3 runs and passed all 18/18 individual assertions (100%), with high-confidence judgments and no low-confidence flags. without_skill failed to meet the expected output in all 3/3 runs (0/3) and failed all 12 assertions evaluated for it (0%), also with high-confidence judgments (meaning the evaluator was confident in scoring these as failures, not that the measurement is shaky). Every individual assertion shown (ordering of levels, and presence of CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/INFO) follows the same pattern: with_skill passes, without_skill fails — this is a broad, consistent gap across all six assertion types rather than an isolated case, and no assertion passed for neither or failed for both, so each assertion is genuinely discriminating here.

Quality comparison could not be assessed: all 3 pairs were skipped, with zero pairs evaluated, so there is no side-by-side quality judgment available to weigh against the assertion results.

Output consistency was measured only for with_skill, which was rated fully "consistent" across all 3 dimensions with high confidence. without_skill has no consistency data (null), so its run-to-run stability is unknown rather than confirmed good or bad.

On runtime and cost, with_skill averaged 3 seconds and $0.03 per run, while without_skill averaged 0 seconds and $0.00 — suggesting without_skill's runs may have terminated immediately or trivially rather than actually producing the expected content, which would be consistent with its 0% pass rates. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.6% vs 3.6%), with no compaction for either.

Overall, this is not a close tradeoff: on the one dimension where both variants were directly and repeatedly measured (expected output and assertions), with_skill passed consistently and without_skill failed consistently across every run and every assertion checked. However, quality-comparison data is entirely missing (skipped), and without_skill's near-zero runtime/cost combined with total assertion failure suggests it may not have engaged with the task the same way with_skill did, which is worth investigating directly rather than assuming it reflects a deliberate quality difference.

firehose-review-pillars.summary:
This eval tested a chat task where the agent was expected to name the AWS Well-Architected Framework pillars (security, reliability, performance, service quotas, cost optimization, operational excellence, sustainability). The trigger condition fired in all 3 runs, meaning the behavior under test was exercised for both variants.

Expected-output and per-assertion results show a stark, consistent split: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%) with high confidence, while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%), also with high confidence in that judgment — so this is not a low-confidence artifact. This pattern repeats identically across all 7 underlying assertions (naming each of the 7 pillars), each evaluated with the LLM evaluator: with_skill passed all 21 assertion instances (21/21), without_skill failed all 21 (0/21). None of the assertions passed for both variants and none failed for both — every single assertion follows the same with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern, indicating without_skill's responses in this eval consistently omitted or misnamed the pillars in a way that failed every check, rather than one variant being marginally weaker.

On efficiency metrics, the two variants were essentially even: both averaged ~4s runtime, with cost slightly lower for with_skill ($0.03 vs $0.04) and context utilization slightly lower for without_skill (3.6% vs 4.6%); neither had any context compaction. These differences are small and not decisive given the large gap on correctness.

Quality comparison data is not available — all 3 pairs were skipped, so no head-to-head quality judgment can be drawn from that dimension.

Output consistency (how stable each variant's responses were across repeated runs) was rated "mostly_consistent" for both, with without_skill scoring somewhat higher (2.67, with 2 dimensions fully consistent and 1 mostly consistent) than with_skill (2.0, with 1 consistent, 1 mostly consistent, and 1 inconsistent dimension), both at high confidence. This suggests without_skill was somewhat more stable run-to-run in how it formatted or structured its answers, even though the content of those answers did not satisfy the expected-output check in any run.

Overall, the dominant signal in this eval is the complete divergence on correctness (expected output and all assertions), which is measured with high confidence and is not explained by trigger or confidence issues. Runtime/cost differences are minor, quality comparison data is absent, and consistency scores show without_skill slightly more stable in output structure despite failing the correctness checks — a tradeoff worth noting rather than a single overall verdict.
